slides.title: What you actually need to install, and what you don't
slides.text: Installing means copying a program into your computer so it lives there. It's not an innocent step. Every installed program takes up disk space and updates itself every few weeks. Sometimes it asks for the admin password. And every once in a while it clashes with something else you had. So every install is a small debt you pay off later. You pay it the day something stops working and you don't know which of the six…
items: Rubén's video told him to install Node.js, Git, Visual Studio Code, and two extensions before writing a single line. Between downloads, restarts, and one wrongly checked box, ninety minutes were gone. The website he ended up building three…

slides.title: Practice: Check the one thing you truly need today: an up-to-date browser
slides.text: In Chrome, click the three vertical dots top right, go into "Help" then "About Google Chrome." That screen checks for updates on its own the moment you open it. If a blue "Relaunch" button shows up, click it and let it restart. In Edge the path is three dots, "Help and feedback," "About Microsoft Edge." Safari updates with the system: Apple menu, "System Settings," "General," "Software Update." Write down the…
items: In your browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari
A message like "Google Chrome is up to date" with a version number underneath. If it asked you to restart and you did, going back into that same screen should now say it's current.

slides.title: Your first project folder
slides.text: A project isn't an idea with files scattered around it. It's a folder, and everything the project needs lives inside it. The test is simple. Copy that folder onto a USB stick and take it to another computer. If it works there, you had a project. If something gets left behind when you copy it, you didn't have a project. For example, an image that was in Downloads, or a text you had on the Desktop. Those are loose…
items: Javi zipped his citas-fisio folder into a 380 KB ZIP and sent it to his nephew to take a look. His nephew opened it and everything was in there. While the project lived on the Desktop there was no way to send it: it was fourteen files…

slides.title: Practice: Pick the project name and write it correctly
slides.text: Write your project's name following three rules. Two words at most. All lowercase, joined by a hyphen. And it should describe WHAT it is, not what it's built with. citas-fisio, climbing-shop, or client-schedule work. my-react-project doesn't, because in a year the technology will be different and the name will lie. No accents, no special characters, no spaces, no capital letters. Under twenty characters. You're…
items: In a note on your phone or on paper, without opening any app yet
A single line, something like citas-fisio. If it has a space, a capital letter, or an accent, rewrite it before moving on. If it's over twenty characters, trim it.

slides.title: What localhost is and how to see your project running
slides.text: When you type amazon.com, your browser sends a request out through your router. That request travels to a data center hundreds of miles away. There, a running computer sends the page back. Localhost is exactly the same thing, with one difference: the computer sending the page back is yours, the one in front of you. The word localhost literally means "this machine." Its number equivalent is 127.0.0.1, an address…
items: Nacho sent his brother the link http://localhost:3000 hoping for feedback on the catalog. His brother replied "I'm getting an error." Neither of them had done anything wrong: on his brother's phone, localhost means his brother's phone.

slides.title: Practice: Ask the AI for your project's startup sheet
slides.text: Open the conversation where the AI created your project (if you have several, the most recent one) and paste the prompt below. What you want isn't a nice explanation, but four specific facts you'll use every day. Which folder to be in, what to type to start it, what exact address to open, and how to stop it. When it answers, don't close that response: you'll need it in the next task.
items: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, in the conversation where you're building your project

A five-line list with a real folder path (something like C:\Users\yourname\projects\bikes). Plus a startup command (almost always npm run dev) and an address with the port included (http://localhost:3000). No filler paragraphs.

slides.title: API keys: what they are and how not to leak them
slides.text: An API key is the password one program uses to talk to another program. It's a string of letters and numbers, something like sk-ant-api03-J9xK7mQ2 plus ninety more characters. It looks like a password, but it works in a much more dangerous way. When you log into your bank they ask for a username, a password, and a code sent to your phone: three things. The key doesn't ask for any of that, because it's username,…
items: The prefixes give away who each key belongs to. Anthropic's start with sk-ant-api03-. OpenAI's, with sk-proj-. Google's, with AIza. Stripe's, which move real money, with sk_live_. Those prefixes aren't decoration: they're exactly what the…

slides.title: Practice: Ask the AI which keys your idea actually needs
slides.text: Open a new conversation and paste the prompt below with the blank filled in. Don't get any key yet. The goal of this task is to avoid ending up with six accounts and cards set up for a project that needs just one key, or none. Read the whole answer before touching anything.
items: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini text box

A short list, usually one to three keys. For each one it'll tell you the company name, the exact address where you get it, and whether it needs a card. With luck, a line telling you that you don't need any to get started.

slides.title: GitHub: saving your work with a reverse gear
slides.text: When you save a file in your folder or in Drive, the new version overwrites the old one. GitHub works the other way around. Every time you upload changes, GitHub saves a complete snapshot of the project at that instant. The snapshot carries the date, your name, and a note you write explaining what you touched. That snapshot is called a commit. The previous snapshot doesn't get deleted or replaced: it stays whole in…
items: A website project with 40 files and 300 KB of code barely takes up any space. With 200 commits stacked on top, on GitHub it weighs less than two phone photos. The history doesn't fill up and doesn't expire: it's text, and text weighs…

slides.title: Practice: Create your GitHub account
slides.text: Go to github.com and click "Sign up," top right. It'll ask you three things in a row, one screen each: email, a password, and a username. The password needs at least 15 characters, or 8 if you mix in a number and a lowercase letter. The username only allows letters, numbers, and hyphens: no spaces, no accented characters. That name shows up in the address of all your projects. Pick something short and presentable,…
items: In your browser, at github.com

You land on a dashboard with a green button that says "Create repository" or "New." To confirm it worked, type github.com/YOUR-USERNAME into the browser bar: your profile should show up, empty but yours, with your name at the top.

slides.title: What would prevent your project from being handed off?
slides.text: Use one case you actually observed. Name the evidence, the risk and the next check. There is no automatically correct option for this open question.
items: Missing evidence
Unreliable repeated event
Unknown permission
No recovery owner
